message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and obligations that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and federal law. For specific situations—especially those involving disputes, evictions, or health and safety concerns—consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written move‑in inventory.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | | **Habitability** | • Landlords must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after notice. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or pursue a lawsuit. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are limited to **$25** per day for a single late payment, or **$50** for multiple late payments. | • Pay on time; if late, negotiate a payment plan. | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease must be in writing if it lasts longer than one year.
• The landlord cannot change the lease terms without your consent. | • Review the lease carefully before signing. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords cannot enter the unit without **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any unannounced entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income (e.g., Section 8). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must provide a **written notice** (30 days for nonpayment, 60 days for lease violations, 90 days for no‑cause termination).
• Eviction must go through the court; landlords cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond to notices promptly; seek legal counsel if you believe the eviction is unlawful. | | **Health & Safety** | • Landlords must comply with local building codes, fire safety regulations, and the Texas Health and Safety Code. | • Report violations to local health or building departments. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, provided you give notice and keep receipts. | • Keep documentation of the defect, notice, and repair costs. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent‑control laws**. | • Your rent is governed solely by the lease agreement. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • The lease may restrict subletting; if it does, you must obtain written permission. | • Negotiate sublet terms with the landlord. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify which utilities you pay. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide renter’s insurance, but it is highly recommended. | • Obtain coverage for personal property and liability. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for breach of contract, damages, or unlawful eviction.
• Small claims court handles disputes up to $20,000. | • File a claim in the appropriate county court. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask about habitability** – confirm that all major systems (plumbing, heating, electrical) are functional. 3. **Verify the security deposit limit** – ensure it does not exceed one month’s rent. 4. **Check for hidden fees** – e.g., pet fees, parking, or “late fee” caps. 5. **Confirm the notice period for termination** – 30/60/90 days depending on the reason. 6. **Document the unit’s condition** – take photos and create an inventory list. --- #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Possible Outcome | |-------|------------|------------------| | Landlord refuses to make repairs | Send a written notice (email or certified mail) detailing the problem and requesting repair within a reasonable timeframe. | Landlord may comply; if not, you can withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct claim. | | Unlawful eviction notice | Verify the notice type and required days. Contact a local tenant‑rights group or attorney. | You may contest the eviction in court. | | Discrimination claim | File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD. | Potential investigation and legal action against the landlord. | | Security deposit dispute | Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | If the deduction is unlawful, you can sue for the full deposit. | --- #### Resources - **Texas Property Code** – the statutory framework for landlord‑tenant relations. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – handles discrimination complaints. - **HUD** – federal agency for housing discrimination and fair housing. - **Local tenant‑rights organizations** – e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local bar associations. - **Small Claims Court** – for disputes under $20,000. --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, a fair security‑deposit process, protection from discrimination, and a clear, lawful eviction procedure. Keep records, communicate in writing, and seek professional help if you encounter problems.
